topic.title: Concept Learning and Compositional Generalization
topic.overview: This broad foundations cluster examines what a learner represents as a concept and how learned knowledge transfers to new combinations. Historical examples concern rules, hypothesis filtering, noisy data, and comparisons of supervised methods. Recent representatives formalize disentanglement, diversity, and the statistical conditions needed to compose knowledge across distributions.
topic.whyItMatters: Terms such as concept, factor, or composition can refer to different mathematical objects. Clear definitions help distinguish a genuine transfer ability from success caused by more data, easier examples, or a favorable evaluation protocol.
topic.evolution: The collection reaches back to rule and pattern learning in 1983. Later titles emphasize statistical rule induction and empirical classifier comparison. The available recent abstracts focus on unifying definitions of disentanglement and separating data limitations from compatibility between a learning algorithm and a composition rule; they do not establish a direct historical dependency.
openQuestions: Which definitions of disentanglement are appropriate for stochastic rather than deterministic representations?
How can experiments isolate knowledge composition from ordinary distributional coverage?
